title: Universal Alignment cannot be measured deterministically, so the framework treats it as a contested spectrum
content:
A.0.1.1.5 makes an unusual admission for a governance framework: Universal Alignment is a spectrum, actors are more or less aligned, and while "in theory Universal Alignment is absolute, in practice it cannot be measured deterministically and thus practically will always be subject to debate and changes over time."

Rather than defining a metric, Alignment Engineering targets the *derivative*: it "aims to minimize the degree that actors experience their own, and others', Universal Alignment changing over time." Stability of alignment is the engineering objective, because the level itself is unobservable.

The Assumption itself then supplies what measurement cannot: the outcomes of Alignment Engineering — the Artifacts or rules — are held to **always** have the spirit of serving human values and the public good within their context. This is a deliberate axiom, and it is what licenses spirit-of-the-rule interpretation: if a rule's intent is assumed benign by construction, then a reading that contradicts the intent can be treated as an error in the text rather than a valid outcome.
description: The Universal Alignment Assumption concedes alignment is unmeasurable in practice and always subject to debate; Alignment Engineering aims to minimize how much it drifts over time.
